claim: Short-term forecasts of infectious disease burden can contribute to situational awareness and aid capacity planning.
source: Short-term forecasts of infectious disease burden can contribute to situational awareness and aid capacity planning.
evidence: This is a general statement about the utility of forecasts, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: One can maximise the predictive performance of infectious disease forecasts if multiple models are combined into an ensemble.
source: Based on best practice in other fields and recent insights in infectious disease epidemiology, one can maximise the predictive performance of such forecasts if multiple models are combined into an ensemble.
evidence: This statement references best practices and recent insights, drawing on established knowledge.

claim: The European COVID-19 Forecast Hub collected weekly forecasts for COVID-19 cases and deaths for 32 countries over 1-4 weeks from March 2021.
source: We invited groups globally to contribute weekly forecasts for COVID-19 cases and deaths reported by a standardised source for 32 countries over the next 1–4 weeks. Teams submitted forecasts from March 2021 using standardised quantiles of the predictive distribution.
evidence: This describes the data collection methodology of the study.

claim: Each week an ensemble forecast was created where each predictive quantile was calculated as the equally-weighted average of all individual models' predictive quantiles.
source: Each week we created an ensemble forecast, where each predictive quantile was calculated as the equally-weighted average (initially the mean and then from 26th July the median) of all individual models' predictive quantiles.
evidence: This describes the methodology for creating the ensemble forecast.

claim: The ensemble method changed from using the arithmetic mean to the median from 26th July 2021 onwards.
source: From 08 March 2021, we used the arithmetic mean. However we noticed that including highly anomalous forecasts in a mean ensemble produced extremely wide uncertainty. To mitigate this, from 26th July 2021 onwards the ensemble instead used a median of all predictive quantiles.
evidence: This describes a methodological change made during the study period.

claim: Over 52 weeks, forecasts were collected from 48 unique models.
source: Over 52 weeks, we collected forecasts from 48 unique models.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of models contributing to the study.

claim: 29 models' forecast scores were evaluated in comparison to the ensemble model.
source: We evaluated 29 models' forecast scores in comparison to the ensemble model.
evidence: This describes the scope of the evaluation performed.

claim: The ensemble performed better on relative WIS than 83% of participating models' forecasts of incident cases across all horizons and locations.
source: Across all horizons and locations, the ensemble performed better on relative WIS than 83% of participating models' forecasts of incident cases (with a total N=886 predictions from 23 unique models)
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the performance evaluation.

claim: The ensemble performed better on relative WIS than 91% of participating models' forecasts of deaths across all horizons and locations.
source: and 91% of participating models' forecasts of deaths (N=763 predictions from 20 models).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the performance evaluation.

claim: Ensemble performance declined with longer forecast periods when forecasting cases across a 1-4 week time horizon.
source: Across a 1–4 week time horizon, ensemble performance declined with longer forecast periods when forecasting cases
evidence: This describes a trend observed in the performance data.

claim: Ensemble performance remained stable over 4 weeks for incident death forecasts.
source: but remained stable over 4 weeks for incident death forecasts.
evidence: This describes a trend observed in the performance data.

claim: In every forecast across 32 countries, the ensemble outperformed most contributing models when forecasting either cases or deaths.
source: In every forecast across 32 countries, the ensemble outperformed most contributing models when forecasting either cases or deaths, frequently outperforming all of its individual component models.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the performance results.

claim: The ensemble frequently outperformed all of its individual component models.
source: In every forecast across 32 countries, the ensemble outperformed most contributing models when forecasting either cases or deaths, frequently outperforming all of its individual component models.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the performance results.

claim: The most influential and best choice for ensemble methods was to use a median average of models instead of using the mean, regardless of methods of weighting component forecast models.
source: Among several choices of ensemble methods we found that the most influential and best choice was to use a median average of models instead of using the mean, regardless of methods of weighting component forecast models.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing different ensemble methods.

claim: Combining forecasts from individual models into an ensemble improves predictive performance across epidemiological targets and populations during infectious disease epidemics.
source: Our results support the use of combining forecasts from individual models into an ensemble in order to improve predictive performance across epidemiological targets and populations during infectious disease epidemics.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results.

claim: Median ensemble methods yield better predictive performance than ones based on means.
source: Our findings further suggest that median ensemble methods yield better predictive performance more than ones based on means.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing ensemble methods.

claim: Forecast consumers should place more weight on incident death forecasts than incident case forecasts at forecast horizons greater than 2 weeks.
source: Our findings also highlight that forecast consumers should place more weight on incident death forecasts than incident case forecasts at forecast horizons greater than 2 weeks.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the observed differences in forecast performance.

claim: Researchers, policy makers, and the general public have used epidemiological forecasts to understand and respond to the global outbreaks of COVID-19.
source: Researchers, policy makers, and the general public have used such forecasts to understand and respond to the global outbreaks of COVID-19 (Van Basshuysen et al., 2021; CDC, 2020; European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2021c).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other work.

claim: Forecasters use a variety of methods and models for creating and publishing forecasts, varying in both defining the forecast outcome and in reporting the probability distribution of outcomes.
source: At the same time, forecasters use a variety of methods and models for creating and publishing forecasts, varying in both defining the forecast outcome and in reporting the probability distribution of outcomes (Zelner et al., 2021; James et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other work.

claim: A consistent approach to forecasting across Europe can support accurately informing cross-European monitoring, analysis, and guidance.
source: In this case, a consistent approach to forecasting across the continent as a whole can support accurately informing cross-European monitoring, analysis, and guidance (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2021c).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents a policy rationale.

claim: Some independent forecasting models have produced multi-country results for COVID-19.
source: Some independent forecasting models have sought to address this by producing multi-country results (Aguas et al., 2020; Adib et al., 2021; Agosto and Giudici, 2020; Agosto et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to other work.

claim: Variation in forecast methods and presentation makes it difficult to compare predictive performance between forecast models.
source: Variation in forecast methods and presentation makes it difficult to compare predictive performance between forecast models, and from there to derive objective arguments for using one forecast over another.
evidence: This is a statement about challenges in the field, representing established knowledge.

claim: A forecast hub is a centralised effort to improve the transparency and usefulness of forecasts by standardising and collating the work of many independent teams.
source: A 'forecast hub' is a centralised effort to improve the transparency and usefulness of forecasts, by standardising and collating the work of many independent teams producing forecasts (Reich et al., 2019a).
evidence: This definition is supported by a citation.

claim: The approach to creating a forecast hub was pioneered in climate modelling and adapted for collaborative epidemiological forecasts of dengue and influenza in the USA.
source: The underlying approach to creating a forecast hub was pioneered in climate modelling and adapted for collaborative epidemiological forecasts of dengue (Johansson et al., 2019) and influenza in the USA (Reich et al., 2019a; Reich et al., 2019b).
evidence: This historical context is supported by citations.

claim: Evidence from previous efforts in multi-model infectious disease forecasting suggests that forecasts from an ensemble of models can be consistently high performing compared to any one of the component models.
source: Evidence from previous efforts in multi-model infectious disease forecasting suggests that forecasts from an ensemble of models can be consistently high performing compared to any one of the component models (Johansson et al., 2019; Reich et al., 2019b; Viboud et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Weather forecasting has a long-standing use of building ensembles of models using diverse methods with standardised data and formatting in order to improve performance.
source: Elsewhere, weather forecasting has a long-standing use of building ensembles of models using diverse methods with standardised data and formatting in order to improve performance (Buizza, 2019; Moran et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to work in weather forecasting.

claim: The European COVID-19 Forecast Hub is a project to collate short-term forecasts of COVID-19 across 32 countries in the European region.
source: The European COVID-19 Forecast Hub (European Covid-19 Forecast Hub, 2023d) is a project to collate short-term forecasts of COVID-19 across 32 countries in the European region.
evidence: This is a description of the project being reported on.

claim: The Hub is funded and supported by the ECDC.
source: The Hub is funded and supported by the ECDC
evidence: This is a statement about the project's funding.

claim: The primary aim of the Hub is to provide reliable information about the near-term epidemiology of the COVID-19 pandemic to the research and policy communities and the general public.
source: with the primary aim to provide reliable information about the near-term epidemiology of the COVID-19 pandemic to the research and policy communities and the general public (European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, 2021c).

claim: The Hub aims to create infrastructure for storing and analysing epidemiological forecasts made in real time by diverse research teams and methods across Europe.

source: Teams could express their uncertainty around any single forecast target by submitting predictions for up to 23 quantiles (from 0.01 to 0.99) of the predictive probability distribution.

source: No restrictions were placed on who could submit forecasts.

source: Teams submitted a broad spectrum of model types, ranging from mechanistic to empirical models, agent-based and statistical models, and ensembles of multiple quantitative or qualitative models (described at European Covid-19 Forecast Hub, 2023a).

claim: Forecasts were collected weekly in real time over the 52-week period from 08 March 2021 to 07 March 2022.
source: We collected forecasts submitted weekly in real time over the 52-week period from 08 March 2021 to 07 March 2022.

claim: All forecasts, metadata, and evaluations are freely available and held on Github and Zoltar.
source: All forecasts, metadata, and evaluations are freely available and held on Github (European Covid-19 Forecast Hub, 2023d) (archived in real-time at Sherratt, 2022), and Zoltar, a platform for hosting epidemiological forecasts (EpiForecasts, 2021; Reich et al., 2021).

claim: The WIS is a strictly proper scoring rule.

claim: The WIS encourages forecasters to report predictions representing their true belief about the future.

claim: The relative WIS is computed using a pairwise comparison tournament where for each pair of models a mean score ratio is computed based on the set of shared targets.
source: The relative WIS is computed using a pairwise comparison tournament where for each pair of models a mean score ratio is computed based on the set of shared targets.

source: We scaled the relative WIS of each model with the relative WIS of a baseline model, for each forecast target, location, date, and horizon.
